title: Joy and ease
hookLine: steps five and six: breathing with gladness, breathing with ease

cards: Meditation has a reputation a bit like flossing. Good for you, mildly unpleasant, something to get through. So it's a surprise when the Buddhist breathing discourse, at step five, says: breathe with joy.
And at step six: breathe with ease. Not grim endurance. Gladness.

There's a story behind that, one you already know from camp two. A young man, starving himself in the forest, suddenly remembers a happy afternoon from long ago, and asks himself a question that changes everything.

teach.h: WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT PLEASURE?

teach.b: In the Mahasaccaka Sutta, after he has pushed his body through harsh practice to the edge of death, the Buddha-to-be recalls a day long before: sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father was busy, slipping into a quiet, happy stillness.
And he asks: why am I afraid of that pleasure? It has nothing to do with craving or harm. That question turned him toward the middle way.
Steps five and six carry the same insight. The person trains: experiencing joy, I will breathe in and out. Experiencing ease, I will breathe in and out.
Today's word is piti, joy or rapture: the bright, lifting, sometimes tingling gladness that can arise when the mind settles.
Its partner is sukha, a softer happiness, ease, contentment. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual, tells them apart with a picture.

teach.h: THE POOL SEEN, THE POOL REACHED.
teach.b: A traveler lost in the desert, exhausted, sees a pool of water up ahead: that's piti, the thrill.
Then he reaches it, drinks and bathes: that's sukha, the deep ease. Both are welcome; both are part of the path. You don't manufacture these feelings.
When the body settles, as in steps three and four, pleasure tends to show up on its own: warmth, lightness, a quiet smile. The practice is to let it in, instead of brushing it off as a distraction.
If you've learned to trust only effort and discomfort, that can be the hard part. The discourse trains the other way.

how: Following these steps, Buddhist meditation teachers encourage students to notice and allow the joy (piti) and ease (sukha) that arise as the mind settles, rather than treating practice as grim effort.

o: the bright gladness when the mind settles
the pleasure of getting what you crave

games.q: what's inside the steps — tap the pairs.

s: Buddhist meditation is meant to feel grim
steps five and six are breathing with joy and breathing with ease.
the rose-apple memory led the Buddha to ask why he feared that pleasure
in the Mahasaccaka Sutta, that question turned him toward the middle way.
piti and sukha are exactly the same
piti is the thrill of seeing the pool; sukha is the ease of drinking from it.

games.q: you're meditating, and a warm, happy feeling rises. what do the steps suggest?
o: push it away as a distraction.
let it be felt, and breathe with it.
chase it and try to make it bigger.
games.why: steps five and six train you to breathe experiencing joy and ease: let it in without chasing it.

practice: Let the body settle, then look for anything pleasant, however small: the warmth of your hands, the softness of the out-breath, the quiet in the room, the relief of sitting down.
Don't create anything; when you find something already there, let it be felt fully for a breath or two. If nothing seems pleasant, notice what's neutral and easy; that counts too.

wordCard.voice: Piti. Joy, gladness, the bright lift that can come when the mind settles. Step five of the breath.

carryVoice: Your line: you're allowed to enjoy it. Even the Buddha-to-be had to learn that one. A hundred and ten days now.
